lesson.title: Control which work happens

steps.headline: An if chain runs the first branch whose condition is true, and skips the rest.

lead.text: if, elif and else are branches. Python tests each condition in order and runs only the first one that is true. == compares two values; a single = stores a value.
Put the narrow condition first when ranges overlap.
The conditions are tested from the top. Only one fee is ever assigned.

reveal.text: You followed the chain down. The first condition failed and the second held, so the third branch never ran.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

steps.headline: A for loop takes each item in turn, and range stops before its stop value.

lead.text: for item in range(1, 6) gives item the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The start is included and the stop is not. A running total, called an accumulator, starts before the loop and grows inside it.

steps.headline: Find total after total = 0 and for item in range(1, 6): total += item.

workedSteps.text: range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The stop, 6, is excluded.
total starts at 0, then grows by each item.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
items = list(range(4))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
items = list(range(1, 8, 2))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

steps.headline: Find total after total = 0 and for item in range(3, 12, 3): total += item.

workedSteps.text: range(3, 12, 3) starts at 3 and steps by 3. It stops before 12. How many times does the loop run?
The items are 3, 6 and 9. Add them to total. What is total at the end?

lead.text: A while loop tests its condition before every pass. The body must eventually make the condition false, or the loop never finishes.

reveal.text: You counted the passes by testing the condition each time. The last value crosses the limit, because the test only happens before a pass.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 2
    turns += 1

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 3
    turns += 1

lead.text: and, or and not combine true-or-false tests. On whole numbers, & works on binary digits instead: it keeps a bit only if both numbers have it set.

reveal.text: Each test came out True or False before the words and, or and not combined them. & and | on integers work bit by bit, which is a different job.

lesson.orientation: Trace branches, ranges, loop updates and Boolean conditions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A car park charges £2 for a stay under 1 hour and £5 for a stay under 3 hours. Longer stays cost £9.

intro.promise: By the end you'll trace which branch of an if chain runs and how many times a loop repeats.

recap.keyIdea: A chain runs the first true branch, a for loop visits each item once, and a while loop tests its condition before every pass.

blocks.text: You priced the car park stay at £5 and followed a fee chain to £2. The loop over range(3, 12, 3) ran 3 times and totalled 18.

recap.nextHook: Next: package a calculation as a function you can call again.

questions.prompt: A fee is 0 when units >= 10, otherwise 2 when units >= 5, otherwise 4. What is the fee for 7 units?
hints: Stop at the first condition that holds.
Check units >= 10 before units >= 5.
For 7 units, follow the first true condition to its fee.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first condition is false and the second true, so the fee is 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The first condition fails for 7 and the second holds, so the chain stops there.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs 10 units or more. For 7 units the first condition fails.
That is the else branch. The second condition already held, so else never ran.

hints: The stop value is excluded.
Start at 2 and keep adding the step.
List the generated values below 9 and add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The range contains 2, 4, 6 and 8; their sum is 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. The range holds 2, 4, 6 and 8, and sum adds them.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes 10. The range stops before 9.
Start the list at 2, not 3. Count 2, 4, 6, 8.

questions.prompt: Start count = 0 and turns = 0. While count < 7, add 2 to count and add 1 to turns. What is turns at the end?
hints: Test the condition before each pass.
Write the values of count: 0, then 2, and so on.
Stop when count is no longer below 7, and count the passes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: count reaches 2, 4, 6 and 8, so the body ran 4 times.

questions.onCorrect: 4. count goes 2, 4, 6, 8. At 6 the test still passed, so one more pass ran.

misconceptions.feedback: At 6 the condition count < 7 is still true, so there is one more pass.
That is the final value of count. The question asks how many passes ran.

questions.prompt: With x = 6, how many of these are True: x > 3 and x < 9, x > 8 or x < 2, not x > 5?
hints: Work out each part separately, then combine them.
and needs both parts true. or needs one.
not flips True and False.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first is True; the second and third are False.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Only the first holds: 6 is above 3 and below 9. The other two come out False.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the third: x > 5 is True, so not x > 5 is False.
The first test holds: 6 is above 3 and below 9.
or needs one true part, and neither part of the second is true.

questions.prompt: Start x = 2. While x < 10, add 3 to x. What is x when the loop stops?
hints: Test the condition before each update.
Write the values: start at 2 and keep adding 3.
Stop after the first value that fails x < 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The updates produce 5, 8 and 11. At 11 the condition is false.

questions.onCorrect: 11. The values are 5, 8, then 11, and 11 fails the test, so the loop ends there.

misconceptions.feedback: At 8 the condition x < 10 still holds, so one more addition happens.
x never equals 10 here. It jumps from 8 over the limit.

questions.prompt: What is 5 & 3 when both operands are integers?
hints: Compare aligned binary digits.
Write both numbers in binary with the same width.
Keep only the bits that are set in both.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In binary, 5 is 101 and 3 is 011. Their shared set bit is 001, which is 1.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Written in binary, 5 and 3 share only the last bit.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. & compares their binary digits.
That is 5 × 3. & keeps only bits set in both numbers.

hints: Is 2 hours under 1 hour?
Is it under 3 hours?
Pick the first charge whose limit the stay fits under.
questions.prompt: What does a 2-hour stay cost, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 hours is not under 1 but is under 3, so the charge is £5.

questions.onCorrect: £5. Two hours is not under 1 hour but is under 3, so the second charge applies. An if chain checks in that order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the under-1-hour charge. A 2-hour stay is longer than that.
That is for longer than 3 hours. A 2-hour stay is shorter.

hints: Which sign is used to compare, and which to store?
questions.prompt: What does the single equals sign do in units = 5?

choices.label: Tests whether units is greater than 5

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A single = is an assignment; comparison uses ==.

questions.onCorrect: It stores 5 under the name units. Comparing two values takes a double equals sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Checking is done with a double equals sign. One sign stores a value.
Greater than is written with its own symbol. The single equals sign stores.

hints: Recall how slices treat their stop position.

choices.label: Only if a step is given

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stop value is not included in the range.

questions.onCorrect: No. range stops before its stop value, so range(2, 6) gives 2, 3, 4 and 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Like a slice, range includes its start and excludes its stop.
The step only sets the gap between values. The stop is always excluded.

hints: What would the total be before any item has been added?

choices.label: So the first item is added to nothing
So the loop knows when to stop

acceptedIdeas: So the first item is added to nothing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Starting the total at 0 means nothing extra is included before the first item.

questions.onCorrect: A total starts at 0 so the first item is added to nothing and does not change the result.

misconceptions.feedback: This range started at 1. The 0 is for the running total, not the range.
The loop stops when the range is used up. The 0 is the starting total.

hints: List the values: begin at the start and add the step each time.
Stop before 12.
Count the values you listed.
questions.prompt: How many times does the loop run?
questions.onCorrect: 3. The range gives 3, 6 and 9, so the body runs once for each.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts 12. The stop value is excluded.

hints: Add the items one by one to a total that starts at 0.
The items are 3, 6 and 9.
Work out 3 + 6 + 9.
questions.prompt: What is total at the end?
questions.onCorrect: 18. The loop added each item to total in turn.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes 12, which is excluded. The range stops before 12.
That is only the last item. The total adds every item.
